questions.stem: A senior engineer wrote the team's TypeScript conventions (error handling, import order, barrel files) in their own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Everything works on their machine, but teammates report that Claude Code ignores the conventions. What is the cause, and the fix?

options.text: User-level memory isn't shared. Move the conventions into the project CLAUDE.md (repo root or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) and commit it.
options.why: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` lives only on one machine. Project memory is shared through version control.

options.text: Teammates need to run `/memory` once after pulling, so Claude Code re-indexes and picks up the new conventions file.
options.why: `/memory` shows and edits memory files. It can't load a file that only exists on another machine.

options.text: Each teammate should copy the file into their own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so every machine has the same user-level memory.
options.why: This works temporarily, but the copies drift and aren't version-controlled.

options.text: The conventions belong in `.claude/settings.json`, which is the shared configuration file that Claude Code reads for team-wide behaviour.
options.why: `settings.json` holds permissions, hooks and environment settings. Conventions belong in memory (CLAUDE.md or rules).

questions.explanation: User scope (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) is personal. Team conventions belong in project-scoped CLAUDE.md committed to the repo.

questions.stem: Testing conventions (fixtures, naming, mocking rules) apply to every `*.test.ts` and `*.spec.tsx` file. Those files are spread across about 40 directories in all apps and packages. What is the most maintainable way to have Claude Code apply the conventions only when they are relevant?

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md to each directory that contains tests, and add a CI check that fails if a new test directory lacks one.
options.why: This duplicates content across 40+ files. The CI check treats the symptom of a poor structure.

options.text: A `.claude/rules/` file whose `paths:` frontmatter globs `**/*.test.ts` and `**/*.spec.tsx`.
options.why: Path-scoped rules load whenever matching files are being worked on, wherever they live.

options.text: A "Testing" section in the root CLAUDE.md that starts with "Apply only when editing test files".
options.why: This is always loaded, which wastes context, and its scoping relies on the model's inference.

options.text: A project skill `/testing-conventions` that engineers run before they start writing or modifying tests.
options.why: Skills need invocation, so the conventions wouldn't apply automatically.

questions.explanation: Use `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` globs for conventions that cut across the directory structure. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files suit conventions that follow the directory tree.

questions.stem: The platform team wants every engineer to have a `/new-endpoint` command that scaffolds an API route following house conventions. They want updates to reach everyone automatically. Where should the command live?

options.text: In each engineer's `~/.claude/commands/new-endpoint.md`, distributed by a bootstrap script in the repo that engineers re-run after updates.
options.why: This is personal scope with manual syncing, so updates won't reach everyone automatically.

options.text: In a `## Commands` section of the root CLAUDE.md that describes the steps and the trigger phrase `/new-endpoint`.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is memory. It doesn't define slash commands.

options.text: In `.claude/commands/new-endpoint.md` inside the repository, committed with the code.
options.why: Project-scoped commands are shared with everyone who clones the repo, and they update through git.

options.text: In an MCP server that the platform team hosts, which exposes `new-endpoint` as a prompt to all connected clients.
options.why: Possible, but it is heavier infrastructure than a committed command file for a repo-specific workflow.

questions.explanation: Shared slash commands go in the project's `.claude/commands/` directory. Personal ones go in `~/.claude/commands/`.

questions.stem: A `/audit-deps` skill reads hundreds of lockfile entries and changelogs, then produces a half-page report. Engineers say that after running it, their main session feels sluggish and forgets earlier work. Which SKILL.md frontmatter change best addresses this?

options.text: Limit `allowed-tools` to `Read` and `Grep`, so the skill can't run commands that produce large amounts of output.
options.why: This restricts tool access, but the skill still reads hundreds of files into the main context.

options.text: Add an `argument-hint` asking for a single package name, so engineers audit one dependency at a time.
options.why: This changes usage, not where the verbose work accumulates, and loses the full audit.

options.text: Set `context: fork`, so the skill runs in an isolated context and only its report returns to the session.
options.why: A forked context isolates verbose work from the main session.

options.text: Add an instruction to the skill body telling Claude to run `/compact` immediately after producing the report.
options.why: Compacting afterwards is lossy, and the earlier work has already been crowded out.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` runs a skill in its own context so that verbose intermediate work doesn't pollute the caller's session.

questions.stem: An engineer must migrate 120 files from a deprecated logging library to a new one. The team hasn't decided between a thin adapter (fast, keeps the old API) and a full call-site rewrite (cleaner, riskier). How should Claude Code be used?

options.text: Use direct execution with a detailed prompt describing both strategies, and let Claude pick the better one as it migrates.
options.why: The strategy choice gets made implicitly, file by file, instead of being decided first.

options.text: Use plan mode to explore usage and settle the strategy and plan, then switch to direct execution to migrate in batches.
options.why: Large, multi-file work with an architectural choice benefits from planning before execution.

options.text: Stay in plan mode for the entire migration, including the edits, so every change is reviewed against the plan as it is made.
options.why: Plan mode is for investigation and design. The implementation happens in execution.

options.text: Have an Explore subagent catalogue the call sites, then let the engineer apply a codemod without using Claude for the decision.
options.why: This discards Claude's help with the strategy decision and the semantic differences.

questions.explanation: Use plan mode for large-scale or architectural work and for choosing between approaches, then direct execution for the changes.

questions.stem: An engineer asks Claude Code to rename a misspelled local variable (`recieved` → `received`) inside one 30-line function. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Plan mode first, so Claude can check whether the same misspelling appears elsewhere before changing anything.
options.why: That's overkill for a local rename the engineer has already scoped.

options.text: Direct execution, since the change is small, local and well specified.
options.why: Planning overhead isn't justified for a trivial, clear edit.

options.text: A forked session, so that the rename can be discarded easily if it breaks anything unexpected.
options.why: A fork adds nothing that version control and the edit itself don't already provide.

options.text: An Explore subagent that maps every reference, followed by direct execution with the subagent's list.
options.why: This is unnecessary indirection for a variable that is local to one function.

questions.explanation: Match the mode to the task: direct execution for simple, well-scoped changes.

questions.stem: Claude Code keeps using `moment.js`, which the team banned a month ago. The engineer suspects an old memory file is still being loaded from somewhere in the hierarchy. What is the fastest way to find out?

options.text: Search the repository and home directory for every file named CLAUDE.md, and open each one to look for moment.js references.
options.why: This works but is slow, and it can miss imported files.

options.text: Start a session with debug logging enabled and read the startup log to see which configuration files were parsed.
options.why: This is indirect. A built-in command already answers the question.

options.text: Run `/memory` to list the loaded memory files, and open the offending one for editing.
options.why: `/memory` is the built-in way to inspect and edit loaded memory.

options.text: Run `/compact` and read the generated summary, which lists the instructions currently influencing the session.
options.why: `/compact` compresses conversation history. It doesn't list memory sources.

questions.explanation: `/memory` shows the loaded memory hierarchy and is the standard diagnostic.

questions.stem: The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines covering API style, Terraform, frontend patterns and release processes. Engineers notice that instructions near the middle are often ignored. What is the best restructuring?

options.text: Keep shared essentials in CLAUDE.md with `@` imports, and move area-specific conventions to `.claude/rules/` or subdirectory CLAUDE.md files.
options.why: Modular organisation keeps always-loaded context small and relevant.

options.text: Keep a single file but rewrite it as terse bullet points without examples, cutting it to about 300 lines.
options.why: Examples often carry the most value, and the file stays monolithic and always loaded.

options.text: Convert each section into a skill, so that only the relevant conventions load when an engineer invokes them.
options.why: Skills are on-demand, so conventions that must always apply would be missed.

options.text: Move the most frequently ignored sections to the top and bottom of the file, where the model attends most reliably.
options.why: Reordering is a partial mitigation. The file is still bloated and loaded in full every time.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md supports modular organisation through `@import`, `.claude/rules/` and directory-level files. Keep what is always loaded lean.

questions.stem: Claude keeps generating date-formatting helpers that mishandle the team's edge cases (fiscal years, ISO weeks, user time zones), despite two paragraphs of prose describing the rules. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Rewrite the prose more precisely, using RFC-style MUST and SHOULD language for each rule, and ask Claude to re-read it before coding.
options.why: Prose that is more formal can still be ambiguous. Concrete cases remove the ambiguity.

options.text: Give 2–3 concrete input/output examples or failing tests for the edge cases, and iterate until they pass.
options.why: Concrete examples and test-driven iteration remove the ambiguity that prose leaves.

options.text: Turn on extended thinking, so Claude reasons more carefully through the existing description before writing code.
options.why: More reasoning over an ambiguous specification doesn't reveal the intended behaviour.

options.text: Ask Claude to generate five alternative implementations, then pick whichever one looks closest to the intent.
options.why: This produces variety without a criterion. Tests or examples are what supply the criterion.

questions.explanation: Iterative refinement works best with concrete examples and tests. The interview pattern also helps with ambiguous requirements.

questions.stem: After two hours exploring the billing module, Claude Code's answers are vaguer and it has started contradicting conclusions it reached an hour ago. The engineer still needs to implement a change based on those findings. What should they do?

options.text: Persist the key findings to a notes file (or `/compact`), then continue from that summary or in a fresh session that reads it.
options.why: Persisting findings and compacting counters context degradation in long sessions.

options.text: Continue, but restate the most important earlier conclusions in each new prompt so they stay near the end of the context.
options.why: This helps marginally, but the degraded, bloated context remains.

options.text: Paste the full billing module source into the chat again so Claude has fresh, complete information to reason from.
options.why: This adds more bloat and makes the degradation worse.

options.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window and replay the session, so nothing from the exploration is lost.
options.why: This is costly, and a larger window doesn't stop attention from diluting over a long session.

questions.explanation: In long explorations, persist findings (scratchpad files), compact or summarise, and continue in a fresh context.

questions.stem: Before changing the auth flow, an engineer wants Claude to survey how 30 services call the auth library. They don't want the main session to fill up with grep output and file contents. What is the best approach?

options.text: Run the searches in the main session but ask Claude to keep only a running summary in its replies, ignoring the raw output.
options.why: The raw output still enters the context. Asking Claude to ignore it doesn't remove it.

options.text: Run the survey in the main session, then run `/compact` before starting on the auth change itself.
options.why: This works, but it pollutes the context first and loses detail during compaction.

options.text: Delegate the survey to a subagent, such as Explore, that works in its own context and returns a concise structured summary.
options.why: Subagent delegation isolates verbose discovery from the main context.

options.text: Ask Claude to read the auth library's own source first, and infer from it how services are likely to call it.
options.why: Inference isn't a survey, so it will miss real-world call patterns.

questions.explanation: Use subagents to explore and summarise, so the main session keeps the essential findings.

questions.stem: Yesterday an engineer worked on a feature in a named Claude Code session. Overnight, a teammate merged a large refactor that renamed modules and moved functions across the same files. What is the best way to continue?

options.text: `--resume` the session as-is: Claude Code detects modified files and silently refreshes its view of them.
options.why: Claude would reason from outdated file contents held in its history.

options.text: Fork the session, so yesterday's state is preserved, and continue the work in the fork.
options.why: A fork still inherits the stale context.

options.text: Start fresh with a structured summary of yesterday's decisions, or resume and name the changed files so Claude re-reads them.
options.why: Resumed sessions hold stale file contents. Fresh context, or explicit pointers to the changes, is more reliable.

options.text: Rebase the feature branch onto the old commit locally, so the files match what the session saw yesterday.
options.why: This works against the team's merged work and only postpones the conflict.

questions.explanation: `--resume` is convenient, but after significant external changes either tell the session what changed or start fresh with a structured summary.

questions.stem: An engineer has spent 40 minutes in a session analysing the caching layer. They now want to try two competing implementations from that same point, without either attempt contaminating the other's context. Which feature fits?

options.text: Run `/compact` after the first attempt, then start the second attempt in the same session with the compacted history.
options.why: The compacted summary still carries attempt A's reasoning into attempt B.

options.text: Use plan mode for one implementation and direct execution for the other, so their contexts stay logically separated.
options.why: Modes don't isolate context.

options.text: Open a brand-new session for the second attempt and paste in a summary of the 40-minute analysis.
options.why: This works, but the summary loses detail. Forking is the intended tool.

options.text: Fork the session (`--fork-session` with `--resume`, or `fork_session` in the SDK) and run each attempt in its own branch.
options.why: Forking creates independent branches from a shared starting point.

questions.explanation: Session forking explores alternatives from a common baseline.

questions.stem: The team wants every engineer's Claude Code to connect to the company issue-tracker MCP server. Each engineer has their own API token, and security forbids committing secrets. How should this be configured?

options.text: Commit a project `.mcp.json` that defines the server and references the token as `${TRACKER_TOKEN}`, which each engineer sets locally.
options.why: Shared configuration plus per-user secrets through environment-variable expansion is the standard pattern.

options.text: Have each engineer add the server to their user-level `~/.claude.json`, using their own token, by following a setup page in the wiki.
options.why: It works, but the shared server definition isn't version-controlled and drifts between machines.

options.text: Commit `.mcp.json` with a shared service-account token restricted to read-only scopes, so a leak has limited impact.
options.why: This still commits a secret, and it loses per-user attribution.

options.text: Store the server URL in CLAUDE.md and let Claude prompt each engineer for their token at the start of every session.
options.why: CLAUDE.md isn't MCP configuration, and typing tokens into chat leaks them into transcripts.

questions.explanation: Project scope (`.mcp.json`) is for shared servers and user scope (`~/.claude.json`) is for personal ones. Use `${ENV_VAR}` expansion for secrets.

questions.stem: A multi-hour, multi-phase codebase modernisation keeps losing its place when the session crashes or the context is compacted, and Claude then redoes or skips files. Which TWO practices make the work reliably resumable? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Keep a manifest file of every file or phase with its status, which Claude updates as it works and reads on restart.
options.why: Manifest-based recovery makes progress durable outside the context window.

options.text: Write a short summary of each finished phase to a notes file before starting the next one.
options.why: Summarising before each phase carries the essential state forward compactly.

options.text: Rely on `--resume` after a crash, since it restores the full conversation, including which files were already done.
options.why: Resume restores the conversation, not a reliable progress ledger, and it may carry stale state.

options.text: Raise the output token limit so Claude can process larger batches per turn and finish before compaction is needed.
options.why: Output tokens don't control context growth or crash recovery.

options.text: Run every phase in one continuous conversation, so Claude always has the complete history available for reference.
options.why: That is exactly what causes degradation and fragility.

questions.explanation: Durable external state (manifests, notes) plus phase summaries make long-running work robust.

questions.stem: The team shares a `/review` skill in `.claude/skills/review/`. One engineer prefers a more verbose variant that also explains every suggestion. How should they get it without affecting teammates?

options.text: Edit the shared skill to accept a `--verbose` argument, then commit it, so everyone can opt into the verbose behaviour.
options.why: Reasonable if the team wants it, but it changes the shared asset for a personal preference.

options.text: Create a personal skill with the same name, `review`, in `~/.claude/skills/`, so it overrides the team version locally.
options.why: Reusing the same name creates ambiguity and conflicts. Use a distinct name.

options.text: Create a personal skill under a distinct name, such as `review-verbose`, in `~/.claude/skills/`.
options.why: A personal variant under a distinct name avoids conflicting with the team's shared skill.

options.text: Add "when I run /review, explain every suggestion in detail" to the project's root CLAUDE.md file.
options.why: That affects the whole team and bloats always-loaded memory.

questions.explanation: Keep personal customisations in user scope under distinct names. Project scope is for shared team assets.
